title: The North American martyrs (1640s)
hookLine: Jesuits and lay helpers killed in the Great Lakes region, remembered with the harm of colonization

cards: A French priest with mutilated hands kneels before an altar in France. His captors had cut and chewed his fingers, and the rules of the time said a priest's hands had to be whole to say Mass.
Tradition says the pope gave him permission anyway. Then he did something hard to understand. He went back across the ocean, to the country where he had been tortured, and he was killed there.
His name was Isaac Jogues, one of a group the Church calls the North American martyrs.

teach.b: Jesuit priests, among them Jean de Brébeuf and Isaac Jogues, and lay helpers like René Goupil and Jean de Lalande, who worked among the Wendat people, sometimes called the Huron, around the Great Lakes.
They learned the languages, lived in the villages, wrote reports home. Brébeuf is remembered for a Christmas song in the Wendat language. Second, how they died.
The Wendat and the Haudenosaunee nations, including the Mohawk, were at war, and the French were allied with the Wendat.

teach.h: KILLED IN A WAR OF NATIONS.
teach.b: The missionaries died in that war: some killed in raids, others tortured and killed after capture. Jogues wrote that Goupil was killed for making the sign of the cross over a child.
Catholics honor them as martyrs, who died for the faith they carried and would not abandon their missions.
Jesus says it in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Third, the rest of the story.
The missions came with European contact, and with it diseases that emptied Native villages. Some Wendat blamed the missionaries.
The missions were tied to a French colonial project that, over time, took land and power from Native nations.
The Haudenosaunee weren't villains in a saint's story; they were nations with their own reasons, alliances and dead. Fourth, holding both.
Some Catholics in North America now speak of these martyrs alongside an honest account of colonization.
Courage and harm sit in the same story.

teach.h: LAY DOWN HIS LIFE FOR HIS FRIENDS.
teach.b: Remembering one alone would be untrue.

how: Catholics in the United States and Canada keep a feast of the North American martyrs, with shrines in New York and in Ontario, and some dioceses now pair it with prayer and education about Indigenous history.

o: a Jesuit martyr who went back after torture
a French explorer who mapped the Great Lakes
a Mohawk convert who sheltered missionaries

games.q: the North American martyrs — tap the pairs.
p: killed for a sign of the cross

s: lay helpers like René Goupil and Jean de Lalande are honored with them.
the martyrs died in a war between Native nations allied with different powers
the French were allied with the Wendat, who were at war with the Haudenosaunee.
the missions did only good for the Wendat
European contact brought diseases that emptied Native villages, and the missions were tied to colonial power.

games.q: you're Isaac Jogues, back in France after captivity and torture, with hands that barely work. what do you do?
o: go back to the same country.
games.why: he went back across the ocean, and he was killed there.

practice: In one hand, hold the missionaries: their courage, their love for the people they lived among, their deaths.
In the other, hold the Native nations: the sickness that emptied their villages, the land taken, the wars made worse by powers from across the sea, and notice which hand wants to drop.
If you pray, pray for the dead on every side; if not, hold them all, without choosing.

wordCard.voice: Isaac Jogues. A Jesuit priest tortured and mutilated among the Wendat, who returned to the same country and was killed there, one of the North American martyrs.

carryVoice: Your line: remember all of it. The truest telling keeps everyone in the room. Day eight hundred sixty-two.
